title: The time before
hook: Lucretius: the ages before we were born didn't trouble us, and the ages after won't either
carry: a mirror of the time to come

segments.voice: Yesterday, in a prison cell, Socrates called philosophy a practice of dying. Your line was practice letting go.

Somewhere there's a photograph of your parents, or grandparents, from before you were born. A wedding, a beach, a kitchen with ugly wallpaper. They're laughing at something. The light is the same light. The world is busy and complete, and you are nowhere in it. Is there anything painful in being absent from it? A Roman poet named Lucretius asked a question very like that, and built a whole argument about death on the answer.
screen: `A PHOTO FROM BEFORE YOU.` → `ANYTHING PAINFUL IN THAT?` → `A POET BUILDS ON IT.`

segments.voice: First, the poet. Lucretius wrote a long poem in Latin verse, On the Nature of Things, to explain the teaching of the Greek philosopher Epicurus. In that teaching everything, the soul included, is made of tiny particles, and at death they scatter. No one is left to suffer anything. In the third book he says it in a single line: death is nothing to us. Second, the history lesson. He recalls a terrible time, when Carthage came against Rome from every side and the whole world shook, unsure who would rule land and sea. And we, he says, felt nothing. We weren't there yet. So when we are no longer here, nothing can touch us, not even if earth and sea and sky are thrown together. Third, the mirror. Look back, he says, at the endless ages that passed before we were born. Nature holds that time up to us like a mirror of the time to come after we die. Is there anything frightful in it? Anything gloomy? Isn't it more peaceful than any sleep? Fourth, the honest reply. Not every reader is persuaded. Some answer that what they fear isn't being dead; it's losing this: the people, the morning light, the unfinished things. The mirror doesn't speak to that, and other voices in this block reject Lucretius's view of the soul. But the picture still makes the vast stretch of nothing before you feel familiar, even restful.
screen: `DEATH IS NOTHING TO US.` · `WHEN CARTHAGE CAME, WE FELT NOTHING.` · `THE TIME BEFORE IS A MIRROR.` · `NOT EVERY READER IS PERSUADED.` · then, large: `THE TIME BEFORE.`

segments.voice: Picture a moment from before you were born, a grandparent as a child, a street years before you walked it, a storm nobody remembers now, vivid with weather and sound and people busy with their lives. Notice that you're absent from it, and how that absence feels, calm, strange, or nothing at all, without pushing toward any conclusion. If the time after comes in, let it sit beside the time before, two quiet rooms.
Lucretius, the Roman poet who held up the ages before our birth as a mirror for the time after death. Today's word.
Your line: a mirror of the time to come. The ages before you, held up like glass. Day seven hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Some readers of Lucretius use his mirror as a reflection: they recall the long time before their birth and set it beside the time after death, to see whether the fear changes.
